blocks.text: To say why someone does something, use to + base verb: I went to the chemist's to buy some plasters. She is saving money to visit her cousins in Canada. In order to + base verb means the same and sounds more formal, and in order not to + base verb is the negative: We left home early in order not to miss the train. For goes before a noun, not a verb: I went to the chemist's for some plasters. Do not say for to buy or for buy.
Printed task: Put the bracketed verb into the gap. I'm going to the library to ___ (return) these books before it closes.

Pop out means go out for a short time, usually to do something quick nearby; it is informal and common in British English. Class example: I'm just popping out to get some milk, so I'll be back in ten minutes. Common combinations: pop out for lunch, pop out to the shops.
Someone on the recording says: Actually, I went to the chemist's for to buy some plasters is fine as well; plenty of speakers say it.
Near the end of the recording, someone repeats the model sentence: We left home early in order not to miss the train.

study.imageFa: افرادی که با شتاب در حال بستن در خانه و نگاه کردن به ساعت مچی خود هستند تا مبادا به قطار دیر برسند.
